title: Primary and Secondary Qualities in Early Modern Philosophy

summaries.example: Think about a lemon. Its shape and size stay there even when nobody is looking. But its sour taste happens when the lemon affects a person's tongue and mind. Philosophers ask whether the shape is part of the lemon itself, while sourness is a quality connected with how a lemon affects a taster.
summaries.summary: Early modern philosophers asked which features belong to objects independently of our senses and which depend more closely on sensing. They often called size, shape, extension, motion, position, and sometimes solidity and number primary qualities. They called color, taste, smell, sound, heat, coldness, and touch-related features secondary qualities. This did not mean everyone agreed that secondary qualities were unreal. Some thinkers treated them as sensations, while others treated them as powers or effects connected with objects. Galileo argued that a body could have its basic shape and motion without a perceiver, while a tickle or taste needs a sensing being. Boyle tried to explain qualities through tiny moving parts. Locke connected the distinction to how ideas come from experience. Reid focused on how sensations guide us toward qualities in the world. The entry emphasizes that these philosophers offered different versions and that scholars still debate how to understand them.
key_ideas: Many early modern philosophers divided qualities into primary and secondary kinds.
Primary qualities were usually connected with the body's size, shape, motion, position, or solidity.
Secondary qualities were often explained as effects produced in sensing beings.
Galileo used a thought experiment about touching a statue and a person to support this difference.
Locke made the distinction especially famous, but philosophers disagreed about exactly what it meant.
Boyle and Reid developed other versions, so there was no single agreed-upon doctrine.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps us ask a basic question: how do our experiences connect with the world? It also shows why seeing or feeling something does not automatically tell us exactly what exists outside us. The questions raised by these philosophers connect ideas about perception with scientific explanations of matter, motion, color, sound, and touch.

important_terms.definition: A feature such as size, shape, motion, position, or solidity that philosophers often say belongs to an object itself.
A feature such as color, taste, smell, sound, heat, or coldness that is connected with the way an object affects a living perceiver.
A living being, such as a person or animal, that can sense things through organs such as eyes, ears, skin, or a tongue.
A feature of a thing. Size, shape, color, and taste can all be called qualities.

questions_to_think_about: Would a ball still have a shape if nobody could see or touch it?
Is sweetness in a piece of candy, in the taster, or in the relationship between them?
Can our senses tell us what a thing is like by itself?
Why might scientists want to explain colors or sounds using tiny parts and motion?

summaries.example: Imagine a fire warming your hand. A Galileo-style account says that the fire's size, shape, and motions can cause a warming sensation in a being with skin, but warmth as felt is not simply another shape or motion inside the fire. A Locke-style account distinguishes the sensation in the mind from the body's power to produce it. The example shows why philosophers must distinguish an experienced quality, its physical cause, and the language used to describe both.
summaries.summary: The primary-secondary quality distinction developed through seventeenth- and eighteenth-century attempts to explain matter, perception, and scientific knowledge. Primary qualities were commonly associated with extension, size, figure, position, motion, and sometimes solidity and number. Secondary qualities included color, taste, odor, sound, heat, coldness, and tactile features. The central issue was not simply whether secondary qualities are real. It was whether they are intrinsic features of bodies, powers grounded in bodily structure, relations between bodies and perceivers, or sensations occurring in minds. Galileo's argument begins with what can and cannot be conceived as absent from a body and uses examples such as tickling to connect secondary qualities with sentient organisms. Boyle's corpuscular theory explains qualities through the mechanical features and arrangements of tiny parts, while leaving interpretive problems about relational and dispositional qualities. Locke makes the distinction part of an account of human ideas: primary qualities are inseparable from bodies, whereas secondary qualities are powers to produce ideas through primary features. His resemblance thesis says that ideas of primary qualities resemble bodily qualities, while ideas of secondary qualities do not, though the meaning of 'resemble' is disputed. Reid rejects the theory that we immediately perceive mental ideas. He distinguishes sensations from perceptions and says that primary qualities are known more directly and distinctly, while secondary qualities are known through their effects on us. The entry presents these as historically related but importantly different theories.
key_ideas: The primary-secondary distinction concerns both what exists in bodies and how sensory knowledge gives access to it.
Galileo treats primary features as necessary for conceiving bodies, while tastes, odors, sounds, and similar effects depend on sensory systems.

Boyle's corpuscular theory explains qualities through mechanical affections such as size, shape, motion, and texture, but scholars debate whether qualities reduce to these features or remain relations.
Locke distinguishes ideas in the mind from qualities or powers in objects and argues that ideas of primary qualities resemble their causes more closely than ideas of secondary qualities.
Reid separates sensations from perceptions: sensations are felt effects, while perception involves conceiving and believing in an external quality.
The philosophers disagree about whether secondary qualities are sensations, dispositions, unknown physical causes, or relations involving perceivers.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate sits at the intersection of metaphysics, epistemology, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of science. It asks whether perception reveals the world as it is, how physical explanations relate to conscious experience, and how ordinary language can blur distinctions between an object, its effects, and our ideas. It also illustrates why a famous philosophical division may have several competing foundations rather than one canonical meaning.

important_terms.definition: A quality treated as intrinsic to material bodies and intelligible through features such as extension, size, figure, position, motion, or solidity.
A quality treated as derivative, perceiver-related, or a power of bodies to produce sensations through their primary features.
A feature or capacity attributed to a substance or body; the term can refer either to an intrinsic feature or to a power to affect something.
A capacity of a body to produce an effect, such as a sensation or a physical change in another body.
A theory explaining observable changes through matter's small parts, their sizes, shapes, arrangements, and motions.
A mental experience or act produced in a perceiver; philosophers disagreed about whether it represents an external quality and how it does so.
A relation in which an idea is said to match or share a relevant feature with what causes or is represented by it.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining a color through bodily structure show that color is unreal, or only that its cause is different from its appearance?
What is the difference between a body's power to produce warmth and the warmth someone feels?
Can an idea represent an external cause while still being confused about that cause?
Does the fact that a sensation varies with a perceiver show that the external quality is mind-dependent?
Why might the same word, such as 'red' or 'hot,' be used for both an experience and something attributed to an object?

summaries.example: Suppose two students taste the same apple. One thinks it is very sweet, while the other has a cold and tastes little sweetness. The apple still has a particular size, shape, and motion of its parts. Philosophers might say its sweetness is a power to affect tasters, or they might focus on the sweet experience itself. The disagreement is about what the word 'sweet' names.
summaries.summary: The entry examines a long-running philosophical distinction between primary and secondary qualities. Primary qualities are usually listed as size, shape, extension, duration, position, motion, and sometimes solidity or number. They are commonly described as objective features of material bodies. Secondary qualities include colors, tastes, odors, sounds, heat, coldness, and tactile features. These are often described as less independent of perceivers, but philosophers explain that dependence in different ways. Galileo argues that a body cannot be conceived without its basic measurable features, whereas a color, taste, smell, or tickle requires a sensory system. His approach connects perception with a new kind of natural philosophy based on measurement, hypotheses, and mechanical causes. Boyle develops a corpuscular account: bodies have tiny parts with mechanical features, and their arrangements produce powers or qualities. A major question is whether a quality is nothing beyond those mechanical features or is a relation involving more than one body. Locke's influential version distinguishes an idea, which occurs in the mind, from a quality, understood as a power in an object to produce an idea. He says primary qualities are inseparable from bodies and that ideas of them resemble their causes, while secondary qualities do not resemble what exists in bodies. Reid takes a different route. He says sensations are felt effects, while perceptions involve an external object and belief in its existence. Primary qualities are known more directly, while secondary qualities are known mainly through the sensations they cause. The entry stresses that these theories overlap but should not be treated as identical.
key_ideas: The distinction separates features thought to belong to bodies from features tied more closely to perception.
Galileo argued that bodies need basic measurable features, but tastes, smells, sounds, and tickles require sensory beings.
Boyle explained qualities using the size, shape, motion, and texture of tiny particles, but his theory leaves open whether qualities are relations or reduced physical features.
Locke distinguished ideas in the mind from powers in objects and made the distinction part of his theory of knowledge.
Reid said sensations are not the same as perceptions: a sensation is felt, while perception presents an external quality as existing.
The entry describes disagreements among philosophers and among modern scholars about what secondary qualities really are.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it concerns how our minds connect with physical things. It helps explain why an object can have measurable features while also producing different experiences in different people. It also shows how philosophy and science can approach the same question differently: philosophy examines concepts such as quality, power, and perception, while natural philosophy seeks physical causes. Understanding the debate makes it easier to notice when everyday words describe an object, an effect, or an experience.

important_terms.definition: A feature thought to belong to a physical object whether or not anyone senses it, especially size, shape, position, motion, extension, or solidity.
A feature often explained through an object's effects on a perceiver, such as color, taste, smell, sound, heat, or coldness.
A capacity to bring about an effect, such as causing a sensation in a person or changing another object.
A theory that explains bodies and their changes through tiny parts, their arrangements, and their motions.
An experience produced through sensing; some philosophers treated it as a mental effect, while others said it helps direct us toward an external quality.
A feature or capacity attributed to an object or substance. Philosophers disagreed about whether secondary qualities are qualities in the strict sense.

questions_to_think_about: If a sound is not heard, does it still exist as a sound or only as a physical cause of sound?
Is color a feature of an object, a sensation, a power, or more than one of these?
Why would a philosopher separate an object's qualities from the ideas those qualities cause?
Could a physical explanation of taste tell us everything about tasting?
Which seems more convincing: the view that we directly perceive objects, or the view that we first perceive ideas in our minds?
